claim: Adult-onset rapamycin treatment extended the lifespan of wDah females with a log-rank test p-value of 7.4E-08.
source: Adult-onset rapamycin treatment extended the lifespan of wDah females (log-rank test, p=7.4E-08).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (log-rank test) of lifespan data shown in Figure 1A and referenced in the text.

claim: Expression of H3 and H4 in dissected intestines of wDah controls significantly increased with age.
source: Expression of H3 and H4 in dissected intestines of wDah controls significantly increased with age.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Rapamycin substantially increased the expression of H3 and H4 in intestine (n = 4 biological replicates of 10 intestines per replicate, two-way ANOVA, H3 and H4, age p<0.05, treatment p<0.001, interaction p>0.05).
source: Rapamycin substantially increased the expression of H3 and H4 in intestine (n = 4 biological replicates of 10 intestines per replicate, two-way ANOVA, H3 and H4, age p<0.05, treatment p<0.001, interaction p>0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data and two-way ANOVA statistical analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The intestine had much lower basal expression of H3 and H4 than did the other three tissues (brain, muscle, fat).
source: The intestine had much lower basal expression of H3 and H4 than did the other three tissues (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: In the intestine, rapamycin increased expression of histone proteins by 2 days after the start of treatment.
source: In the intestine, rapamycin increased expression of histone proteins by 2 days after the start of treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Expression of H3 and H4 in dissected brain, muscle, or fat of wDah control flies did not change significantly with age or rapamycin treatment.
source: Expression of H3 and H4 in dissected brain, muscle, or fat of wDah control flies did not change significantly with age or rapamycin treatment (n = 4 biological replicates of 10 tissues per replicate, two-way ANOVA, H3 and H4, age p>0.05, treatment p>0.05, interaction p>0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data and two-way ANOVA statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Rapamycin treatment did not affect the expression of H3 and H4 transcripts in the intestine of young flies at 1, 2, and 5 days of age.
source: Rapamycin treatment did not affect the expression of H3 and H4 transcripts in the intestine of young flies at 1, 2, and 5 days of age (n = 3–4 biological replicates of 15 intestines per replicate, two-way ANOVA, age p>0.05, treatment p>0.05, interaction p>0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data and two-way ANOVA statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Rapamycin treatment attenuated the age-associated increase in H3 and H4 transcripts in the intestine of flies at 30 days and 50 days of age.
source: Rapamycin treatment attenuated the age-associated increase in H3 and H4 in the intestine of flies at 30 days and 50 days of age (n = 3–4 biological replicates of 15 intestines per replicate, two-way ANOVA; H3 and H4, age p<0.001, treatment p<0.001, interaction, p<0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data and two-way ANOVA statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Dietary restriction (DR) did not influence the expression of H3 and H4 in intestine.
source: DR (1× vs. 2× SYA food) did not influence the expression of H3 and H4 in intestine (n = 4 biological replicates of 10 intestines per replicate, two-way ANOVA, H3 and H4, age p<0.001, treatment p>0.05, interaction p>0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data and two-way ANOVA statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Rapamycin treatment did not alter the ratio of intestinal cell types.
source: Rapamycin treatment did not affect the proportion of the four cell types (EC, ISCs + EB, EE), but reduced ISC mitosis (n = 6 intestines per condition; two-way ANOVA; rapamycin ECs, ISCs + EBs, EEs p>0.05, Mitosis-ISCs, p<0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data and two-way ANOVA statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Rapamycin treatment did not affect EC polyploidy.
source: Rapamycin treatment did not affect EC polyploidy (n = 5 intestines per condition; n = 12–15 ECs were observed per intestine, data points represent the average value per intestine; two-way ANOVA; rapamycin, p>0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of EC ploidy and two-way ANOVA statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Adult-onset cycloheximide treatment (1 mM) blocked increased expression of histones H3 and H4 in response to rapamycin treatment in intestines of flies at 2 days of age.
source: Adult-onset cycloheximide treatment (1 mM) alone had no effect on histone expression but blocked increased expression of histones H3 and H4 in response to rapamycin treatment in intestines of flies at 2 days of age (n = 4 biological replicates of 10 intestines per replicate, two-way ANOVA, interaction, H3 p<0.05, H4 p<0.01; post-hoc test, *p<0.05, **p<0.01, ***p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data and two-way ANOVA statistical analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Adult-onset, enterocyte (EC)-specific knock-down of eIF3d by RNAi blocked increased expression of H3 and H4 in response to rapamycin treatment in intestine of flies at 20 days of age.
source: Adult-onset, enterocyte (EC)-specific knock-down of eIF3d or eIF3g by RNAi alone had no effect on histone expression but blocked increased expression of H3 and H4 in response to rapamycin treatment in intestine of flies at 20 days of age (n = 4 biological replicates of 10 intestines per replicate, two-way ANOVA, interaction, eIF3d RNAi H3 p<0.01, H4 p<0.001; eIF3g RNAi H3 p<0.05, H4 p<0.05; post-hoc test, *p<0.05, **p<0.01, ***p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data and two-way ANOVA statistical analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Adult-onset, EC-specific knock-down of eIF3g by RNAi blocked increased expression of H3 and H4 in response to rapamycin treatment in intestine of flies at 20 days of age.
source: Adult-onset, enterocyte (EC)-specific knock-down of eIF3d or eIF3g by RNAi alone had no effect on histone expression but blocked increased expression of H3 and H4 in response to rapamycin treatment in intestine of flies at 20 days of age (n = 4 biological replicates of 10 intestines per replicate, two-way ANOVA, interaction, eIF3d RNAi H3 p<0.01, H4 p<0.001; eIF3g RNAi H3 p<0.05, H4 p<0.05; post-hoc test, *p<0.05, **p<0.01, ***p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data and two-way ANOVA statistical analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Adult-onset, EC-specific knock-down of eIF4e by RNAi increased expression of H3 and H4 to the same extent as did rapamycin treatment, with no additional effect of their combination in intestine of flies at 20 days of age.
source: Adult-onset, EC-specific knock-down of eIF4e by RNAi alone increased expression of H3 and H4 to the same extent as did rapamycin treatment, with no additional effect of their combination in intestine of flies at 20 days of age (n = 4 biological replicates of 10 intestines per replicate, two-way ANOVA, interaction, H3 and H4 p<0.01; post-hoc test, *p<0.05, **p<0.01, ***p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data and two-way ANOVA statistical analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Adult-onset, knock-down of Atg5 ubiquitously by RNAi had no effect on increased histone expression in response to rapamycin treatment in intestines of flies at 20 days of age.
source: Adult-onset, knock-down of Atg5 ubiquitously by RNAi had no effect on increased histone expression in response to rapamycin treatment in intestines of flies at 20 days of age (n = 4 biological replicates of 10 intestines per replicate, two-way ANOVA, interaction, H3 and H4 p>0.05; post-hoc test, NS p>0.05, **p<0.01, ***p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data and two-way ANOVA statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Adult-onset bortezomib treatment (2 µM) had no effect on increased expression of H3 and H4 in response to rapamycin treatment in intestine of flies at 20 days of age.
source: Adult-onset bortezomib treatment (2 µM) had no effect on increased expression of H3 and H4 in response to rapamycin treatment in intestine of flies at 20 days of age (n = 4 biological replicates of 10 intestines per replicate, two-way ANOVA, interaction, H3 and H4 p>0.05; post-hoc test, NS p>0.05, ***p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data and two-way ANOVA statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Rapamycin treatment did not disturb histone incorporation into chromatin.
source: We observed that histone H3 remained in chromatin in intestines of both control and rapamycin-treated flies (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that rapamycin did not disturb histone incorporation into chromatin.
evidence: The claim is supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The number of mono-, di-, and tri-nucleosomes in the intestine of rapamycin-treated flies was substantially higher than in controls after a short (1 min) MNase digest.
source: The number of mono-, di-, and tri-nucleosomes in the intestine of rapamycin-treated flies was substantially higher than in controls after a short (1 min) MNase digest.
evidence: The claim is supported by MNase digestion assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Over-expression of histones H3 and H4 in ECs elevated the number of nucleosomes in intestines as much as did rapamycin treatment, with no further increase in the combined treatment.
source: Over-expression of histones H3 and H4 in ECs elevated the number of nucleosomes in intestines as much as did rapamycin treatment, with no further increase in the combined treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by MNase digestion assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Rapamycin treatment induced a substantial chromatin rearrangement in ECs, with marked accumulation of chromatin at the nuclear envelope in both young (10-day-old) and middle-aged (40-day-old) flies.
source: Rapamycin treatment induced a substantial chromatin rearrangement in ECs, with marked accumulation of chromatin at the nuclear envelope in both young (10-day-old) and middle-aged (40-day-old) flies (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Knock-down of either histone H3 or H4 in adult ECs by RNAi blocked the rapamycin-induced chromatin rearrangement.
source: Knock-down of either histone H3 or H4 in adult ECs by RNAi blocked the rapamycin-induced chromatin rearrangement (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: EC-specific over-expression of H3 and H4 recapitulated the effect of rapamycin treatment on chromatin arrangement, with no further effect in the presence of rapamycin.
source: EC-specific over-expression of H3 and H4 recapitulated the effect of rapamycin treatment, with no further effect in the presence of rapamycin (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Rapamycin did not affect the amount of HP1, but it altered its distribution, by expanding it across the nucleus in ECs.
source: Rapamycin did not affect the amount of HP1, but it altered its distribution, by expanding it across the nucleus in ECs.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification of HP1 distribution.

claim: Blocking-increased expression of H3 or H4 in response to rapamycin treatment did not affect the amount of HP1 but abolished HP1 expansion to the whole nucleus in response to rapamycin treatment.
source: Blocking-increased expression of H3 or H4 in response to rapamycin treatment did not affect the amount of HP1 but abolished HP1 expansion to the whole nucleus in response to rapamycin treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: Over-expression of H3 and H4 in ECs recapitulated the effect of rapamycin treatment on HP1 distribution, with no additional effect in the presence of rapamycin.
source: Furthermore, over-expression of H3 and H4 in ECs recapitulated the effect of rapamycin treatment on this phenotype, with no additional effect in the presence of rapamycin (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Adult-onset knock-down of H3 or H4 by the 5966GS driver alone had no effect on lifespan of control flies, but completely blocked the lifespan extension by rapamycin.
source: Adult-onset knock-down of H3 or H4 by the 5966GS driver alone had no effect on lifespan of control flies, but completely blocked the lifespan extension by rapamycin (Figure 4A, B; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by lifespan data and log-rank test statistical analysis shown in Figure 4A, B and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Rapamycin treatment reduced pH3-positive cell number in the intestine.
source: In line with the previous study (Fan et al., 2015), rapamycin treatment reduced pH3-positive cell number, a proxy for ISC proliferation (Biteau et al., 2010), in the intestine (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data and quantification shown in Figure 4D-F, and is consistent with a previous study (Fan et al., 2015).

claim: Knock-down of H3 or H4 in adult ECs substantially attenuated the effect of rapamycin on ISC proliferation.
source: Knock-down of H3 or H4 in adult ECs substantially attenuated the effect of rapamycin on ISC proliferation (Figure 4D, E) and on intestinal dysplasia in old flies (50-day-old) (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data and quantification shown in Figure 4D, E, G.

claim: Adult-onset expression of H3/H4 in adult ECs extended lifespan (log-rank test, p=0.001) and had no additional effect on lifespan in the presence of rapamycin (Rapamycin vs. Rapamycin + RU, p=0.48).
source: Adult-onset expression of H3/H4 in adult ECs extended lifespan (log-rank test, p=0.001) and had no additional effect on lifespan in the presence of rapamycin (Rapamycin vs. Rapamycin + RU, p=0.48).
evidence: The claim is supported by lifespan data and log-rank test statistical analysis shown in Figure 4C and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Expression of H3/H4 in adult ECs reduced ISC proliferation in intestine of flies at 20 days of age.
source: Expression of H3/H4 in adult ECs reduced ISC proliferation in intestine of flies at 20 days of age (n = 23–24 intestines, two-way ANOVA, interaction, p<0.001; post-hoc test, ***p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data and two-way ANOVA statistical analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Expression of H3/H4 in adult ECs reduced intestinal dysplasia in 50-day-old flies.
source: Expression of H3/H4 in adult ECs reduced intestinal dysplasia in 50-day-old flies (n = 9–12 intestines, two-way ANOVA, interaction, p<0.01; post-hoc test, ***p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by intestinal dysplasia quantification and two-way ANOVA statistical analysis shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Rapamycin had a substantial impact on the entire transcriptome in the intestine, which increased with age.
source: Rapamycin had a substantial impact on the entire transcriptome in the intestine, which increased with age (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), with modest changes in gene expression at day 10, and substantial changes at days 30 and 50 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data and PCA analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Expression of autophagy-related genes (e.g., Bchs, Diabetes and obesity regulated (DOR), Stat92E, Atg4a, and Atg8a) were affected by rapamycin treatment.
source: Although we did not detect any significant enrichment of specific biological processes by Gene Ontology (GO) analysis, we noticed that expression of autophagy-related genes (e.g., Bchs, Diabetes and obesity regulated (DOR), Stat92E, Atg4a, and Atg8a) were affected by rapamycin treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: EC-specific knock-down of H3 by RNAi abolished the effect of rapamycin on expression of the Bchs and DOR transcripts but not the Stat92E transcript.
source: Quantitative RT-PCR on RNA isolated from fly intestines showed that EC-specific knock-down of H3 by RNAi abolished the effect of rapamycin on expression of the Bchs and DOR transcripts but not the Stat92E transcript (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Over-expression of H3 and H4 altered the expression of Bchs and DOR transcripts similarly to rapamycin treatment, with no additional effect of their combination.
source: Conversely, over-expression of H3 and H4 altered the expression of Bchs and DOR transcripts similarly to rapamycin treatment, with no additional effect of their combination (Figure 5A), suggesting that increased histone expression mediated increased expression of transcripts of autophagy-related genes Bchs and DOR in response to rapamycin.
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Expression of H3/H4 in adult ECs mediated enrichment of H3K4me3, H3K9me3, H3K27me3, and HP1 on Bchs and DOR transcriptional start sites in the intestine of flies at 20 days of age.
source: Expression of H3/H4 in adult ECs mediated enrichment of H3K4me3, H3K9me3, H3K27me3, and HP1 on Bchs and DOR transcriptional start sites in the intestine of flies at 20 days of age (n = 3 biological replicates of 25 intestines per replicate, two-way ANOVA;post-hoc test, compared to controls, *p<0.05, **p<0.01, ***p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data and two-way ANOVA statistical analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: EC-specific expression of H3/H4 did not affect phospho-S6K levels, in either the presence or the absence of rapamycin.
source: As expected, rapamycin greatly decreased phospho-S6K levels, but EC-specific expression of H3/H4 did not affect phospho-S6K levels, in either the presence or the absence of rapamycin (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Rapamycin treatment resulted in hyperphosphorylation of Atg1, shown by a slower-migrating band on western blot.
source: Furthermore, rapamycin treatment resulted in hyperphosphorylation of Atg1, shown by a slower-migrating band on western blot (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B), in line with previous studies (Memisoglu et al., 2019; Yeh et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B and is consistent with previous studies (Memisoglu et al., 2019; Yeh et al., 2010).

claim: EC-specific expression of H3/H4 alone did not cause hyperphosphorylation of Atg1.
source: However, EC-specific expression of H3/H4 alone did not cause this effect (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B.

claim: EC-specific expression of H3/H4 decreased the amount of Atg8a-II and Ref(2)P to the same degree as did rapamycin treatment, with no additional effect of their combination.
source: EC-specific expression of H3/H4 decreased the amount of Atg8a-II and Ref(2)P to the same degree as did rapamycin treatment, with no additional effect of their combination (Figure 5C), suggesting that increased histone expression mimicked the effect of rapamycin treatment on autophagy activation.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Rapamycin treatment increased the number of LysoTracker-stained puncta in intestines.
source: In line with a previous study (Bjedov et al., 2010), rapamycin treatment increased the number of LysoTracker-stained puncta in intestines (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B) while EC-specific knock-down of H3 by RNAi abolished the increase (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B and is consistent with a previous study (Bjedov et al., 2010).

claim: EC-specific knock-down of H3 by RNAi abolished the increase in LysoTracker-stained puncta in response to rapamycin.
source: In line with a previous study (Bjedov et al., 2010), rapamycin treatment increased the number of LysoTracker-stained puncta in intestines (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B) while EC-specific knock-down of H3 by RNAi abolished the increase (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Expression of H3/H4 increased the number of LysoTracker-stained puncta to the same extent as did rapamycin treatment, and neither treatment affected the number of Cyto-ID-stained puncta.
source: Reciprocally, expression of H3/H4 increased the number of LysoTracker-stained puncta to the same extent as did rapamycin treatment, and neither treatment affected the number of Cyto-ID-stained puncta (Figure 5D), suggesting that expression of H3/H4 in ECs did not disturb autophagic flux.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Rapamycin treatment attenuated the age-related loss of the bicellular junctional protein coracle.
source: Rapamycin treatment attenuated the age-related loss of the bicellular junctional protein coracle (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C; Resnik-Docampo et al., 2017; Salazar et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C and is consistent with previous studies (Resnik-Docampo et al., 2017; Salazar et al., 2018).

claim: EC-specific knock-down of H3 by RNAi abolished the effect of rapamycin on maintenance of coracle levels at EC junctions.
source: EC-specific knock-down of H3 by RNAi abolished the effect of rapamycin on maintenance of coracle levels at EC junctions, while expression of H3/H4 resulted in maintenance of coracle similarly to rapamycin treatment, without further effect of their combination (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Expression of H3/H4 resulted in maintenance of coracle similarly to rapamycin treatment, without further effect of their combination.
source: EC-specific knock-down of H3 by RNAi abolished the effect of rapamycin on maintenance of coracle levels at EC junctions, while expression of H3/H4 resulted in maintenance of coracle similarly to rapamycin treatment, without further effect of their combination (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Rapamycin treatment resulted in a reduction of barrier function loss, and this effect was abolished by knock-down of H3 in adult ECs.
source: Rapamycin treatment resulted in a reduction of barrier function loss, and this effect was abolished by knock-down of H3 in adult ECs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Smurf assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Expression of H3/H4 in ECs resulted in a modest, but significant, reduction in the number of Smurf flies and had no further effect in the presence of rapamycin.
source: Expression of H3/H4 in ECs resulted in a modest, but significant, reduction in the number of Smurf flies and had no further effect in the presence of rapamycin (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Smurf assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Reduction of Atg5 substantially reduced the number of LysoTracker-stained puncta following increased expression of H3/H4 in ECs.
source: Reduction of Atg5 substantially reduced the number of LysoTracker-stained puncta following increased expression of H3/H4 in ECs (Figure 6A), suggesting that Atg5 was required for the effect of increased histone expression on autophagy activation.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: EC-specific knock-down of Atg5 alone did not affect lifespan, but it abolished the increase in response to increased expression of H3/H4.
source: EC-specific knock-down of Atg5 alone did not affect lifespan, but it abolished the increase in response to increased expression of H3/H4 (Figure 6B; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 6B and Supplementary file 4.

claim: EC-specific knock-down of Atg5 completely blocked the effects of increased expression of H3/H4 on intestinal dysplasia and maintenance of gut integrity.
source: Furthermore, EC-specific knock-down of Atg5 completely blocked the effects of increased expression of H3/H4 on intestinal dysplasia and maintenance of gut integrity (Figure 6C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by intestinal dysplasia and Smurf assay data shown in Figure 6C, D.

claim: Knock-down of Atg1 inhibited the increase in autophagy in response to over-expression of H3/H4.
source: Knock-down of Atg1 inhibited the increase in autophagy in response to over-expression of H3/H4 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) and blocked the beneficial effects of increased expression of H3/H4 on gut health (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Knock-down of Atg1 blocked the beneficial effects of increased expression of H3/H4 on gut health.
source: Knock-down of Atg1 inhibited the increase in autophagy in response to over-expression of H3/H4 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) and blocked the beneficial effects of increased expression of H3/H4 on gut health (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by intestinal dysplasia data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Reduction of Bchs expression by RNAi in combination with either rapamycin treatment or over-expression of H3/H4 in ECs blocked the increase of LysoTracker-stained puncta in response to H3/H4.
source: Reduction of Bchs expression by RNAi in combination with either rapamycin treatment or over-expression of H3/H4 in ECs blocked the increase of LysoTracker-stained puncta (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A) in response to H3/H4, suggesting that Bchs was crucial for the effects of increased histone expression on autophagy activation.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Knock-down of Bchs alone had no effect on lifespan, but it abolished the effects of both rapamycin treatment and histone over-expression on lifespan.
source: Knock-down of Bchs alone had no effect on lifespan, but it abolished the effects of both rapamycin treatment and histone over-expression on lifespan (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B; Supplementary files 5 and 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B, and Supplementary files 5 and 6.

claim: Knock-down of Bchs abolished the effects of rapamycin treatment and histone over-expression on intestinal dysplasia and gut integrity.
source: It also abolished the effects of these treatments on intestinal dysplasia and gut integrity (Figure 7C, D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by intestinal dysplasia and Smurf assay data shown in Figure 7C, D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: EC-specific over-expression of Bchs was sufficient to recapitulate the effects of rapamycin and histone over-expression on autophagy, lifespan, and intestinal homoeostasis.
source: Conversely, EC-specific over-expression of Bchs was sufficient to recapitulate the effects of these treatments on autophagy, lifespan, and intestinal homoeostasis (Figure 7E–H; Supplementary file 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence, lifespan, intestinal dysplasia, and Smurf assay data shown in Figure 7E-H and Supplementary file 7.

claim: Neither knocking down nor over-expressing Bchs in ECs influenced mTORC1-mediated phosphorylation of Atg1.
source: Moreover, we found that neither knocking down nor over-expressing Bchs in ECs influenced mTORC1-mediated phosphorylation of Atg1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A, B.

claim: Expression of all of the core histones (H2A, H2B, H3, and H4) in the small intestine of female mice was significantly increased by rapamycin treatment at 12 months and 22 months of age.
source: Expression of all of the core histones (H2A, H2B, H3, and H4) in the small intestine of female mice was significantly increased by rapamycin treatment at 12 months and 22 months of age (Figure 8A, B), consistent with our results from flies.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8A, B.

claim: Rapamycin treatment induced a modest, but significant, chromatin rearrangement in epithelial cells in villi, with marked accumulation of chromatin at the nuclear envelope in cells of rapamycin-fed mice at 12 months and 22 months of age.
source: Rapamycin treatment induced a modest, but significant, chromatin rearrangement in epithelial cells in villi, with marked accumulation of chromatin at the nuclear envelope in cells of rapamycin-fed mice at 12 months and 22 months of age (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Rapamycin treatment increased nucleosome occupancy in 22-month-old rapamycin-fed mouse intestines.
source: Rapamycin treatment also increased nucleosome occupancy in 22-month-old rapamycin-fed mouse intestines (Figure 8D).
evidence: The claim is supported by MNase digestion assay data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Expression of Wdfy3 transcript in the small intestine in 22-month-old mice increased in response to rapamycin treatment.
source: Furthermore, expression of Wdfy3 transcript in the small intestine in 22-month-old mice increased in response to rapamycin treatment (Figure 8E).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Histone H3 protein levels decrease in aged yeast.
source: Histone H3 protein levels decrease in aged yeast (Feser et al., 2010), the nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans (Ni et al., 2012), and human senescent cells (Ivanov et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Feser et al., 2010; Ni et al., 2012; Ivanov et al., 2013).

claim: Histone H3 protein levels decrease in the nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: Histone H3 protein levels decrease in aged yeast (Feser et al., 2010), the nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans (Ni et al., 2012), and human senescent cells (Ivanov et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Ni et al., 2012).

claim: Histone H3 protein levels decrease in human senescent cells.
source: Histone H3 protein levels decrease in aged yeast (Feser et al., 2010), the nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans (Ni et al., 2012), and human senescent cells (Ivanov et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Ivanov et al., 2013).

claim: Over-expression of core histones H3 and H4 extended replicative lifespan in yeast.
source: Concordantly, over-expression of core histones H3 and H4 extended replicative lifespan in yeast, potentially attenuating the age-related loss of nucleosomes, transcriptional dysfunction, and genomic instability in aged yeast cells (Feser et al., 2010; Hu et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Feser et al., 2010; Hu et al., 2014).

claim: Lowered activity of the IIS/mTOR network by nutritional, genetic, or pharmacological interventions can extend lifespan and reduce age-related pathologies in multiple organisms.
source: Lowered activity of the IIS/mTOR network by nutritional, genetic, or pharmacological interventions can extend lifespan and reduce age-related pathologies in multiple organisms (Fontana et al., 2010; Kenyon, 2010; Niccoli and Partridge, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Fontana et al., 2010; Kenyon, 2010; Niccoli and Partridge, 2012).

claim: Reduction of mTORC1 activity by genetic manipulation of key components of mTORC1, TOR or Raptor, extends lifespan in yeast, nematode worms C. elegans, the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, and mice.
source: Reduction of mTORC1 activity by genetic manipulation of key components of mTORC1, TOR or Raptor, extends lifespan in yeast, nematode worms C. elegans, the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, and mice (Johnson et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Johnson et al., 2013).

claim: Rapamycin treatment extends lifespan in diverse organisms, including mice, and attenuates a broad spectrum of age-related functional decline and diseases.
source: Rapamycin treatment extends lifespan in diverse organisms, including mice, and attenuates a broad spectrum of age-related functional decline and diseases (Johnson et al., 2013; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Johnson et al., 2013; Li et al., 2014).

claim: Lifespan extension by rapamycin in Drosophila requires reduced S6K activity and increased autophagy downstream of mTORC1.
source: Lifespan extension by rapamycin in Drosophila requires reduced S6K activity and increased autophagy downstream of mTORC1 (Bjedov et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Bjedov et al., 2010).

claim: Genetic manipulations that reduce S6K activity extend lifespan in both Drosophila and mice.
source: Consistently, genetic manipulations that reduce S6K activity (Kapahi et al., 2004; Selman et al., 2009) or activate autophagy (Pyo et al., 2013; Ulgherait et al., 2014) extend lifespan in both Drosophila and mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Kapahi et al., 2004; Selman et al., 2009).

claim: Genetic manipulations that activate autophagy extend lifespan in both Drosophila and mice.
source: Consistently, genetic manipulations that reduce S6K activity (Kapahi et al., 2004; Selman et al., 2009) or activate autophagy (Pyo et al., 2013; Ulgherait et al., 2014) extend lifespan in both Drosophila and mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Pyo et al., 2013; Ulgherait et al., 2014).

claim: Activating expression of autophagy-related genes can prevent age-related dysfunction in a variety of tissues.
source: More generally, activating expression of autophagy-related genes can prevent age-related dysfunction in a variety of tissues; for instance, limiting intestinal barrier dysfunction, memory impairment, and muscular dystrophy in animal models (Hansen et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Hansen et al., 2018).

claim: The Drosophila intestine consists of four major cell types: intestinal stem cells (ISCs), multipotent enteroblasts, secretory enteroendocrine cells, and polyploid ECs.
source: The fly intestine contains four major cell types: intestinal stem cells (ISCs), which are mitotically active throughout the life course, multipotent enteroblasts, secretory enteroendocrine cells, and polyploid ECs that are the major differentiated cell type (Lemaitre and Miguel-Aliaga, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Lemaitre and Miguel-Aliaga, 2013) and established knowledge about Drosophila intestinal anatomy.

claim: Histones can undergo increased translation via a non-canonical, eIF3-mediated mechanism.
source: However, previous studies have demonstrated notable exceptions to this translational suppression, including histones, which can undergo increased translation via a non-canonical, eIF3-mediated mechanism (Lee et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2016; Thoreen et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Lee et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2016; Thoreen et al., 2012).

claim: Inhibition of eIF4 components can enforce mRNA translation through an eIF3-specialised pathway.
source: This result was in line with the previous study showing that inhibition of eIF4 components can enforce mRNA translation through an eIF3-specialised pathway (Lee et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Lee et al., 2016).

claim: ECs play a key role in modulating ageing and age-related pathologies.
source: ECs play a key role in modulating ageing and age-related pathologies (Bolukbasi et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2014; Lemaitre and Miguel-Aliaga, 2013; Resnik-Docampo et al., 2017; Salazar et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Bolukbasi et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2014; Lemaitre and Miguel-Aliaga, 2013; Resnik-Docampo et al., 2017; Salazar et al., 2018).

claim: Age-related intestinal pathologies are driven by both unregulated ISC division and loss of homeostasis in ECs.
source: Age-related intestinal pathologies are driven by both unregulated ISC division (Biteau et al., 2008; Choi et al., 2008) and loss of homeostasis in ECs (Bolukbasi et al., 2017; Resnik-Docampo et al., 2017; Salazar et al., 2018), both of which reduce lifespan.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Biteau et al., 2008; Choi et al., 2008; Bolukbasi et al., 2017; Resnik-Docampo et al., 2017; Salazar et al., 2018).

claim: Rapamycin reduces age-associated ISC proliferation, attenuating intestinal dysplasia.
source: Rapamycin reduces age-associated ISC proliferation, attenuating intestinal dysplasia (Fan et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Fan et al., 2015).

claim: Altered histone modifications (e.g., H3K9me3 and H3K27me3) regulate autophagy-related gene expression.
source: Altered histone modifications (e.g., H3K9me3 and H3K27me3) regulate autophagy-related gene expression (An et al., 2017; Wei et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (An et al., 2017; Wei et al., 2015).

claim: mTORC1 can activate autophagy through transcriptional changes.
source: Lowered mTORC1 activity can activate autophagy, either through transcriptional changes (Martina et al., 2012) or through mediating the phosphorylation status of Atg1, to regulate the activity of the Atg1/ULK1 autophagic complex and subsequent autophagic processes (Jung et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Martina et al., 2012).

claim: mTORC1 can activate autophagy through mediating the phosphorylation status of Atg1.
source: Lowered mTORC1 activity can activate autophagy, either through transcriptional changes (Martina et al., 2012) or through mediating the phosphorylation status of Atg1, to regulate the activity of the Atg1/ULK1 autophagic complex and subsequent autophagic processes (Jung et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Jung et al., 2010).

claim: Activation of autophagy promotes increased intestinal junction and barrier integrity in worms and flies.
source: Activation of autophagy promotes increased intestinal junction and barrier integrity in worms and flies, and these play an important role in healthy longevity (Hansen et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Hansen et al., 2018).

claim: WDFY3 is a cargo adaptor for selective degradation of ubiquitinated protein aggregates and physically interacts with Atg5 and p62.
source: WDFY3 is a cargo adaptor for selective degradation of ubiquitinated protein aggregates and physically interacts with Atg5 and p62 (Clausen et al., 2010; Filimonenko et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Clausen et al., 2010; Filimonenko et al., 2010).

claim: Mutants in the Drosophila Wdfy3 homolog Bchs show shortened lifespan and neurodegeneration.
source: Mutants in the Drosophila Wdfy3 homolog Bchs show shortened lifespan and neurodegeneration (Finley et al., 2003; Sim et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Finley et al., 2003; Sim et al., 2019).

claim: There are many physiological and functional similarities between the fly and mammalian intestine, especially the signalling pathways that regulate intestinal regeneration and disease.
source: There are many physiological and functional similarities between the fly and mammalian intestine, especially the signalling pathways that regulate intestinal regeneration and disease (Apidianakis and Rahme, 2011; Jiang and Edgar, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Apidianakis and Rahme, 2011; Jiang and Edgar, 2012).

claim: Intestinal villi are predominantly composed of ECs.
source: In mammals, intestinal villi are small projections that extend into the lumen of the small intestine, and they are predominantly composed of ECs (Sancho et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Sancho et al., 2015) and established knowledge about mammalian intestinal anatomy.

claim: Rapamycin affects histone methylation and chromatin states in aged mice.
source: Several lines of evidence from previous studies have suggested that rapamycin affects histone methylation and chromatin states in aged mice (Gong et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Gong et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2017).

claim: In humans, rapamycin affects chromatin organisation in fibroblasts from normal individuals in a way that mimics that seen in fibroblasts from centenarians.
source: Furthermore, in humans, rapamycin affects chromatin organisation in fibroblasts from normal individuals in a way that mimics that seen in fibroblasts from centenarians (Lattanzi et al., 2014), further supporting the idea that the mTORC1-histone axis is a pro-longevity mechanism in mammals.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Lattanzi et al., 2014).

claim: Increased histone expression in ECs is a key step for rapamycin-dependent longevity and gut homoeostasis.
source: Increased expression of histones in ECs was a key step for rapamycin-dependent longevity and gut homoeostasis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experimental results showing that blocking histone increase abolishes rapamycin's effects on lifespan and gut health.

claim: Direct expression of H3/H4 in ECs was sufficient to extend lifespan and improve intestinal health during ageing.
source: Importantly, direct expression of H3/H4 in ECs was sufficient to extend lifespan and improve intestinal health during ageing.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that overexpression of H3/H4 in ECs extends lifespan and improves gut health markers.

claim: Increased expression of H3/H4 in ECs activated autophagy by epigenetic, transcriptional regulation of expression of autophagy-related genes.
source: Increased expression of H3/H4 in ECs activated autophagy by epigenetic, transcriptional regulation of expression of autophagy-related genes, including Blue Cheese (Bchs), a selective autophagy cargo adaptor, which we demonstrated to be required and sufficient for the effects of increased histone levels on intestinal autophagy, gut health, and lifespan.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data showing altered histone modifications at autophagy gene loci and qRT-PCR data showing increased expression of autophagy genes.

claim: Bchs is required and sufficient for the effects of increased histone levels on intestinal autophagy, gut health, and lifespan.
source: Increased expression of H3/H4 in ECs activated autophagy by epigenetic, transcriptional regulation of expression of autophagy-related genes, including Blue Cheese (Bchs), a selective autophagy cargo adaptor, which we demonstrated to be required and sufficient for the effects of increased histone levels on intestinal autophagy, gut health, and lifespan.
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic manipulation experiments showing that Bchs knockdown abolishes the effects of increased histones, while Bchs overexpression recapitulates these effects.

claim: The mTORC1-histone axis is at least partially conserved in mammals.
source: In mice, rapamycin treatment increases expression of histone proteins and Wdfy3 transcription, and alters chromatin organisation in the small intestine, suggesting that the mTORC1-histone axis is at least partially conserved in mammals and may offer new targets for anti-ageing interventions.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from mice showing similar effects of rapamycin on histone expression, chromatin organization, and Wdfy3 expression as observed in flies.

claim: Rapamycin treatment increases expression of histone proteins through non-canonical eukaryotic initiation factor 3 (eIF3)-mediated translation in the intestine of Drosophila.
source: Rapamycin treatment increased expression of histone proteins through non-canonical eukaryotic initiation factor 3 (eIF3)-mediated translation in the intestine of Drosophila.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments showing that cycloheximide blocks the increase and that eIF3 knockdown abolishes the rapamycin-induced histone increase.

claim: Rapamycin treatment or over-expression of histones H3 and H4 specifically in the enterocytes (ECs) of the fly intestine caused chromatin rearrangement and heterochromatin relocation in EC nuclei.
source: Rapamycin treatment, or over-expression of histones H3 and H4, specifically in the enterocytes (ECs) of the fly intestine, caused chromatin rearrangement and heterochromatin relocation in EC nuclei.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging showing chromatin accumulation at the nuclear envelope and HP1 redistribution.

claim: The mTORC1-histone axis is a crucial pro-longevity mechanism that can offer new directions for therapeutic anti-ageing interventions.
source: Our findings unveil an mTORC1-histone axis as a crucial pro-longevity mechanism that can offer new directions for therapeutic anti-ageing interventions.
evidence: The claim is based on the collective findings of the study showing that the mTORC1-histone axis mediates longevity and health benefits, and is conserved in mammals.
